definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things naturally tend to get more messy over time.
definitions.example: Your room gets messy on its own, but cleaning it takes effort.

definitions.definition: Requiring a lot of energy to maintain order against the natural tendency toward disorder.
definitions.example: Keeping an ice cube from melting in a hot room uses energy.

definitions.definition: The law of physics that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases over time.
definitions.example: A sandcastle left on the beach will eventually crumble, not build itself up.

definitions.definition: A mathematical measure of how much a system's parts work together as a whole, often linked to consciousness.
definitions.example: A brain has high Φ because its parts are highly interconnected; a pile of sand has low Φ.

definitions.definition: The quality of being logically consistent, orderly, and well-integrated.
definitions.example: A well-organized team works coherently; a chaotic mob does not.

definitions.definition: Systems that maintain order by using energy from their surroundings, like living cells or hurricanes.
definitions.example: A whirlpool in a drain stays organized by using the water's flow energy.

definitions.definition: A measure of how complex a piece of information is, based on the shortest computer program that can produce it.
definitions.example: The number 111111... is simple (low K); a random string of digits is complex (high K).

definitions.definition: A mathematical rule or function that transforms one thing into another, like addition or multiplication.
definitions.example: The 'plus' operator turns 2 and 3 into 5.

definitions.definition: A state or pattern that a system naturally moves toward over time.
definitions.example: A marble in a bowl always rolls to the bottom—that's the attractor.

definitions.definition: Growing extremely fast, where the rate of growth itself increases over time.
definitions.example: A virus spreading where each infected person infects two more is exponential growth.

definitions.definition: Growing at a steady, constant rate.
definitions.example: Saving $10 every week is linear growth.

definitions.definition: The idea that the act of measuring or observing something can change its behavior, especially in quantum physics.
definitions.example: Checking if a light is on by looking at it doesn't change it, but in the quantum world, measuring can affect the result.

definitions.definition: A mathematical description of the probability of where a quantum particle might be found.
definitions.example: Before you look, an electron is like a fuzzy cloud of possibilities; the wave function describes that cloud.

definitions.definition: When a quantum system's wave function suddenly becomes a single definite state upon measurement.
definitions.example: The fuzzy cloud of possibilities 'snaps' into one definite location when you measure it.

definitions.definition: A property that arises from the interaction of simpler parts, not present in the parts alone.
definitions.example: Wetness emerges from many water molecules, but a single molecule isn't wet.

definitions.definition: A mapping between two structures that shows they are essentially the same in form or pattern.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual tracks if every station and connection matches.

definitions.definition: A proposed fundamental field in theophysics that connects physical and moral properties mathematically.
definitions.example: Like a magnetic field affects iron, the χ-field might affect moral coherence.

definitions.definition: Two things that are mirror images or counterparts in a mathematical structure.
definitions.example: Left and right hands are symmetry pairs—they match but are opposite.

definitions.definition: A concept in theophysics that moral choices bend or curve a space of possibilities, similar to how gravity curves spacetime.
definitions.example: A good choice might 'curve' the moral landscape toward order, like a heavy ball curves a rubber sheet.

definitions.definition: A mathematical equation that describes how the state of a system changes over time.
definitions.example: It's like a recipe that tells you how a system will evolve moment by moment.

definitions.definition: Something that increases order, integration, or harmony in a system.
definitions.example: A good leader can be a coherence source for a team, making them work better together.

definitions.definition: Something that decreases order, integration, or harmony in a system.
definitions.example: A bad argument can be a coherence sink, making a group more divided.

definitions.definition: A theorem stating that in any consistent mathematical system, there are true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.example: Imagine a rulebook that can't prove all its own rules are correct—there will always be some truths it can't check.

definitions.definition: A set of basic assumptions (axioms) from which all other truths are logically derived.
definitions.example: Euclidean geometry starts with axioms like 'a straight line can be drawn between any two points.'

definitions.definition: Something that is a basic, fundamental building block of reality, not made of anything else.
definitions.example: In some theories, space and time are ontologically primitive—they just exist, not made of something deeper.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical observer with complete, unbiased knowledge of everything; used as a model for God's omniscience.
definitions.example: Imagine a being who sees every possible outcome of every event perfectly—that's the Terminal Observer.

definitions.definition: The state of knowing everything, past, present, and future.
definitions.example: If you knew every answer to every question, you'd be omniscient.

definitions.definition: A point of view from which measurements are made, like standing still or moving in a car.
definitions.example: From your reference frame on Earth, the Sun moves; from the Sun's, Earth moves.

definitions.definition: The phenomenon where frequently observing a quantum system can prevent it from changing state.
definitions.example: Like watching a pot so closely it never boils—constant observation 'freezes' the system.

definitions.definition: The process of proving a claim wrong by finding evidence against it.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' is falsified by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: An imbalance in knowledge or how we know things, where one side knows more than the other.
definitions.example: A teacher knows the test answers; students don't—that's an epistemological asymmetry.

definitions.definition: The idea that information is the most fundamental thing in reality, more basic than matter or energy.
definitions.example: Some think the universe is like a giant computer where information is the basic stuff.

definitions.definition: The property of being able to tell two things apart; if things are indistinguishable, they are the same.
definitions.example: Two identical twins have low distinguishability; a cat and a dog have high distinguishability.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or foundation on which something else exists or operates.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for plants; a computer's hardware is the substrate for software.

definitions.definition: The four-dimensional fabric of the universe that combines space and time into a single continuum.
definitions.example: Einstein showed that gravity is a curvature of spacetime, like a heavy ball on a rubber sheet.

definitions.definition: In theophysics, the infinite loop of giving and receiving among the three persons of the Trinity, representing perfect love and creativity.
definitions.example: Like a perfect dance where each partner gives and receives endlessly, creating new beauty.

definitions.definition: The tendency of systems to lose coherence over time unless sustained by a grace-like aligning force.
definitions.example: A garden left untended will slowly be overrun by weeds—that's grace drift in action.

definitions.definition: The shortest path between two points in a curved space, like a straight line on a flat surface but curved on a sphere.
definitions.example: Airplanes fly geodesic paths on Earth's curved surface to save fuel.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much knowing one thing tells you about another; shared information between two systems.
definitions.example: If knowing the weather tells you whether you'll need an umbrella, that's high mutual information.

definitions.definition: A phenomenon where two particles become linked so that measuring one instantly affects the other, no matter how far apart.
definitions.example: Like two magic coins that always show opposite sides, even if one is on Earth and the other on Mars.

definitions.definition: Able to be tested and confirmed through observation or experiment.
definitions.example: The claim 'water boils at 100°C' is empirically verifiable by heating water.

definitions.definition: The quality of a claim that can be proven false by evidence; a key feature of scientific theories.
definitions.example: The claim 'all planets orbit the Sun' is falsifiable because you could find one that doesn't.

definitions.definition: Existing before or more fundamentally than something else in the order of reality.
definitions.example: In some views, numbers are ontologically prior to physical objects—they exist as abstract truths first.

definitions.definition: A mathematical system based on three interacting operations or elements, like the Trinity.
definitions.example: A three-way switch that controls a light from three locations is a simple triadic structure.

definitions.definition: The idea that civilizations form and grow around a core of coherence, like crystals forming around a seed.
definitions.example: A city might nucleate around a temple or market, growing outward from that center.
